items.body: Rain falls from your eyes and shapes me like a sculpture Some bands chase the moment; Ghost Fetish sounds like they are scoring something far more enduring: a timeless soundtrack for melancholy, desire, and the strange ache of being seen too clearly. The Seattle trio has certainly caught our interest as one of the most intriguing post-punk, goth, and dream-pop acts in North America right now, especially because their music feels governed by emotion rather than calculation. It does not reach for darkness as decoration. It lets the feeling lead: romantic, wounded, atmospheric, and beautiful in the way certain songs seem to glow longer than the night that made them. On their sophomore album, Sculpture, Ghost Fetish turns longing into a material force. The record circles the desire to be witnessed, touched, remembered, and transformed, but it also understands the danger inside that desire. Across these songs, intimacy becomes performance, romance becomes superstition, and identity becomes something unstable: carved by attention, softened by fantasy, eroded by memory, and remade under the pressure of another person’s gaze. That tension gives Sculpture its emotional pull. The album moves through icy synths, buoyant melodic bass, drum-machine pulse, whispered vocals, and dream-smeared atmospheres without ever sounding like it is chasing a trend or trying to flatter the present tense. Ghost Fetish are making the kind of beautiful, haunted, emotionally resonant music they want to make, and that conviction gives the album its private weather: sensual, bruised, nocturnal, and hard to shake. “Show and Tell” opens Sculpture with a deep, dreamy bassline and a chill that feels both intimate and evasive. The song turns confession into something unstable: a push-pull between wanting to be seen and fearing what exposure might cost. Its synthline has an icy bounce, moving with a sleek mechanical charge while Kevin Fenwick’s shuddering vocal drifts through reverb like a figure half-lit in fog. Ghostly echoes of the vocal return around the edges, repeating fragments back into the mix and deepening the song’s wounded pull. What begins as an invitation becomes something closer to a ceremony of vulnerability, setting up the album’s central tension between desire, performance, and the fear of being fully known. “Someone” softens that tension into a more idyllic, daydreaming pulse. Deep synth sighs, crisp snare, and a gently driving rhythm give the track a suspended romantic glow, while the vocals carry the wounded poise of mid-’80s Cure. Musically, there is a clear kinship with New Order’s Power, Corruption & Lies era: bright but unsettled, melodic but emotionally uneasy. The lyric frames identity as something unstable and aspirational, circling the hope of becoming “someone” through rain, strangers, risk, and reinvention. Its romance arrives through blur and uncertainty, as though transformation can only happen after stepping into the wrong light. The result is less a straightforward love song than a dark pop invocation for self-invention. “Fate” begins with a deep, hollow, metallic knell, an intriguing synth tone that immediately gives the song a subterranean charge. From there, it settles into a dreamy underground atmosphere, like water dripping somewhere in a cavern, with the rhythm pressing forward beneath layers of cold echo. Fenwick’s vocal takes on a more punk-inflected edge here, but it remains languid and dream-smeared, delivering its lines with a drawl that feels both numb and possessed. The lyrics treat fate not as an abstraction but as something physical: poisonous, buried, compulsive, and in need of excavation. In the sequence of Sculpture, “Fate” feels like a descent, pulling the album further below street level into colder, more chemical light. “Big Talk” slows the album into a sleek post-punk sway, trading confrontation for a cooler, more unhurried kind of tension. Its buoyant, high bassline carries a Peter Hook-like melodicism, hovering with the mournful lift of Joy Division’s “Atmosphere” while still moving through Ghost Fetish’s own dreamier palette. The vocals are clipped and almost whispered, giving the song a guarded intimacy rather than an outright sneer. Lyrically, “big talk” becomes a phrase for emotional performance: the things people say to fill the room, to keep from giving too much, or to mistake motion for meaning. There is a hint of Lowlife at their dreamiest in the song’s patient drift, with the arrangement letting space, bass, and understatement do most of the emotional work. “Waterfall” stretches into one of the album’s most immersive pieces, opening with a buzzing synth figure and a tapping beat before a melodic bassline, almost guitar-like in its contour, begins to pull the song forward. Fenwick’s vocal is tender and dream-worn, nearly seductive in its softness, while Riley Jakubowski’s backing-vocal sighs gather around it like mist. The effect is less a burst of drama than a slow deluge on the senses, with each texture adding to the feeling of being submerged in something beautiful and difficult to resist. The song’s imagery of rain, bodies, icons, posters, and sculpture gives the album title one of its clearest emotional shapes: the self as something eroded, polished, and remade by longing. For all its darkness, “Waterfall” feels almost cleansing in its soft embrace. “I Like You” takes one of the simplest possible declarations and makes it feel exposed, strange, and slightly dangerous. The drums and synths move in an interesting shuffle, giving the song a subtle sway beneath its heavy-lidded pace. Fenwick’s vocal lands in a tender, wounded ’80s pop register, the kind of delivery that many modern avant-pop and post-punk groups have returned to for its mix of directness and theatrical ache. Riley Jakubowski’s backing vocals add a soft answering presence, while understated electronic burbling moves in the background without crowding the song’s emotional center. It moves slowly and heavily, but never harshly; its softness is what makes it vulnerable. “I Like You” understands that even the plainest confession can leave the speaker defenseless. “So Lucky” brings a more immediate pulse to the back half of Sculpture, opening with a faster up-and-down synth figure that becomes the song’s backbone. Around it, dreamy sustained flourishes and wounded, somber vocals create a contrast between momentum and ache. Fenwick sings with a seductive bedroom charm, intimate without losing the album’s familiar sense of distance, while Riley Jakubowski’s backing vocals echo certain lines with an almost call-and-response effect. As the song progresses, its textures become more adorned and enchanting, with economical guitar flourishes adding flashes of magic rather than crowding the arrangement. The lyric moves through apartments, streets, brownstones, Brooklyn darkness, and windows, turning luck into a romantic superstition: the hope that timing might mean something, even when longing remains on the other side of the glass. “Look at Me” closes Sculpture with an enchanting synth buzz melody that almost resembles a melodica, its volume decaying with a touch of reverb as it drifts into view. A deep, somber bass melody soon enters, grounded by a rapid beat that gives the song a quiet urgency. The vocals return to a hushed, almost whispered mode, but they occasionally rise into subdued, soaring moments that heighten the lyric rather than overpower it. As a closer, the song circles back to the album’s central demand: to be witnessed, desired, remembered, and changed by attention. Its repetitions feel like longing trying to summon the past back into the present, asking to be looked at again with the same intensity as before. Sculpture ends not with resolution, but with an afterimage: the self shaped by desire, still glowing faintly after the song disappears. Listen to Sculpture below, and order the album here. Sculpture by Ghost Fetish Ghost Fetish celebrates sculpture with an album release show on Friday, June 12th, at Seattle’s Clock-Out Lounge with The Fabulous Downey Brothers and Bijoux. Doors are at 8:30 PM, with the show at 9 PM. They are also scheduled to appear at West Seattle Summer Fest on Friday, July 10th, at 4 PM. items._cn_summary: 这是来自美国西雅图的三人乐队Ghost Fetish的第二张专辑，风格融合后朋克、哥特与梦幻流行。专辑以情感驱动，而非刻意营造黑暗氛围，音乐围绕渴望被注视与亲密关系的张力展开。声响上运用冰冷的合成器、旋律化的贝斯、鼓机脉冲与混响人声，营造出朦胧且带有伤感色彩的氛围。作品在情绪表达上偏向内省与不安，同时保持了旋律性。整体风格在小众暗潮场景中具有一定辨识度，延续了该乐队一贯的感性路线。

items.body:
1970 (April 10th, 1970 – IBC Studios, London)

Negotiations were now underway between Sean Murphy and several labels including Deram, CBS and Harvest, the EMI sub-label that had distributed Volume Two in the UK and already had Kevin Ayers in its stable. “They are still not an attraction in the very top bracket, so it was a pleasant surprise to see major companies throwing in genuinely massive bids earlier this year when the group was looking for a recording deal,” Richard Williams revealed. Ultimately, Soft Machine signed with CBS, but Third was self-financed, taken partly from studio sessions, but also from live recordings (“Facelift”) and edits and loops of tapes made by Mike Ratledge and Hugh Hopper at the home of Bob Woolford, who had let them use his Brenell and Stellavox tape recorders. Such infringements of accepted professional practices were only possible because CBS, having acquired a finished album, were no longer in a position to force the band to comply with them.

The benefit for Soft Machine in terms of artistic freedom is easy to measure. But this has to be balanced against the fact that the production on Third is, to put it bluntly, an unmitigated disaster. IBC, at the time the studio of choice for such notorious perfectionists as The Who and the Bee Gees, are probably less to blame than the band themselves who, in spite of the issues with Volume Two, are again credited as sole producers. The sound suffers from almost constantly saturated low frequencies and extremely vague mediums, the drums are much too low in the mix, as if played behind a closed door; and the organ is deprived of much of its biting impact through overwhelming equalization. Unfortunately the 2007 remaster, while an improvement, fails to rectify this.

What is problematic is that, as well as making the album an uncomfortable listen, its sub-par production lessens the claim, widely held at the time of its release, that Third represented musical state-of-the-art. This claim was based on Soft Machine’s ability, unparalleled among their contemporaries, to draw from and amalgamate an exceptionally wide range of influences. Starting out as a rock band, and then gradually moving towards jazz to invent a uniquely personal, and absolutely valid, British answer to American fusion, Soft Machine went even further, incorporating the influence of Stockhausen’s avant-garde and Terry Riley’s repetitive minimalism. Third’s ‘total’ vision, encompassing the entire spectrum of known musical genres, placed Soft Machine at the forefront of musical “progress” in 1970. However, horizons have since expanded to such an extent, beyond the Western tradition in particular, that this concept of universality has aged considerably.

In his insightful review of Third for Actuel, Paul Alessandrini wrote of “music to really listen to, no longer aiming for a purely physical vibration, more interiorized. Soft Machine have re-thought their musical influences – Riley, Cecil Taylor, Coltrane – to really make them their own, abandoning their aesthetics of random explosion in favor of a much more thought-out approach.” There are still occasional reminders of these sonic excesses that, as Alessandrini noted, had now largely disappeared from their music. Mike Ratledge's lengthy solo introduction to “Facelift” almost sounds like an electric exorcism, as if to rid Soft Machine of what still remains of that violence in order to reinvent their music in a more controlled manner, setting formal perfection as their new objective.

Considered as a whole, Hugh Hopper's piece represents the last remnant of Soft Machine’s early days, when they still favored spirit over form - here found lacking in both sound quality and performance, with a few train wrecks along the way - and were intent on disregarding the accepted rules. “Facelift” includes free sections increasingly at odds with Ratledge’s preoccupation with structure – and while as a keyboard player, he still embodies the band’s more radical leanings, Ratledge’s own compositions reveal a much less iconoclastic temperament. Hopper described his own approach at the time as “halfway between” that of Dean, “whose thing is really total improvisation, without any structure, and on the other extreme, [that of Ratledge] who's into entirely formalized musical forms.

“Moon in June” completes Robert Wyatt’s donation to Soft Machine of the material originally intended for his first solo album in 1968. It is interesting to note that Wyatt does this at the exact point where Soft Machine had shed any remaining reference to pop in their live repertoire. Looking back, Wyatt was certainly justified in saying that his side of Third was “the last chance I had to use all the things we'd done without being a jazz band. I wanted to get twenty minutes of it down somewhere.” And since his colleagues, reluctant to act as mere accompanists, had made no secret of their lack of interest in his songs, he recorded most of “Moon in June” on his own, repeating the modus operandi of the 1968-69 demo. Hugh Hopper and Mike Ratledge’s participation is again limited to the organ solo halfway through (Hopper also plays a short melodic theme earlier in the piece). Elton Dean wasn’t asked to contribute anything – Wyatt’s unconvincing justification being that he “hadn’t yet worked out how to work on [his] stuff with the added wind instruments.”

As there was no mention of this breach of band discipline in the sleeve notes, only the most astute listeners noticed that the organ heard during the first ten minutes was a Hammond rather than Ratledge’s signature Lowrey, that the playing clearly wasn’t Ratledge’s, and that most of the ‘bass’ parts were played on an electric piano. When the truth was finally revealed, Wyatt gave contradictory versions of what had happened – in one interview claiming that Ratledge and Hopper had “refused to play [on “Moon in June”] and I had to play it all myself,” in another that he’d “almost had to force them to get them to play on it, which I thought was rather unfair as I’d done my best to get into the music they were writing.” Probably the most objective and believable of Wyatt’s rationales was that he was “terrified it’d be played wrong” if he didn’t perform it all himself.

To approach “Moon in June” as a ‘message’ song would misrepresent Wyatt’s more mundane intent, insofar as the phonetic qualities of the words often seem to matter more to him than their meaning. In other words, “Moon in June” is above all a musical composition, a suite of instrumental sections, some of which are adorned with melodies and lyrics, and others not. The singing accompanies the music rather than vice-versa. In this respect, outside of a possible rivalry with Elton Dean and Wyatt’s inability to sing while drumming, there was no theoretical incompatibility between Soft Machine’s move towards jazz and the continued presence of Wyatt’s voice (even if limited to the Echoplexed scat singing of his solitary interludes during the band’s concerts). Dispensing with vocals was the single most questionable move in Soft Machine’s entire musical evolution, not to mention one whose commercial consequences cannot be underestimated. In different circumstances, Hugh Hopper would surely have joined Wyatt in lobbying for having at least some vocals, but in addition to his increasingly strained personal relationship with Wyatt, Hopper had at this point completely lost interest in non-instrumental music. “I find that using the human voice means asserting limitations to your music right from the start”, he explained in 1972. “I am more interested in the sounds generated by instruments, or electronic devices, because the possibilities offered by songs are much more limited than when experimenting with sounds.”

Even if there was no future for singing in Soft Machine, “Moon in June” at least offers evidence that Robert Wyatt, in a voice-free context, could still be more than “a session drummer for an interesting new species of jazz groups,” as long as he contributed to the writing. When it came to extended pieces, he could stand comparison with Mike Ratledge, even though he lacked any comparable academic background. In addition to its constant melodic inspiration, “Moon in June” is very skillfully constructed (indeed, its instrumental architecture had remained intact since 1968), and confirms Wyatt’s seemingly innate talent for making a coherent whole out of ill-assorted musical ideas.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑围绕软机器乐队的《Third》展开，该作品融合摇滚、学院派爵士、斯托克豪森前卫派与特里·莱利极简主义，是英国对美式融合乐的独特回应，试图构建涵盖多种已知流派的“整体”音乐视野。专辑由乐队自主制作，虽获艺术表达自由，但制作存在低频饱和、鼓声混音过低、风琴音色被均衡掩盖等问题，2007年重制版也未完全修正。评论指出，其当年被视为前沿的音乐 universality 概念，在后续西方以外音乐视野拓展后已显过时，内容未完结，信息尚不完整。

items.body: Review by andrea — Teodicea is a band from Livorno that came to life in 2020 on the initiative of keyboardist and composer Enrico Filippi after he stepped out from Aliante with whom he had previously recorded two albums. The band's name refers to a theological theory (Theodicy) that shows that it is reasonable to believe in God despite evidence of evil in the world and offers a framework which can account for why evil exists. In 2024 they released an excellent debut album entitled "Il mondo esausto" (The exhausted world) on the independent M.P. & Records label with a line up featuring Enrico Filippi (keyboars, piano), Jacopo Morandi (bass) and Giacomo Putrino (drums, percussion, keyboards). It's a completely instrumental work that might recall some Italian bands of the seventies like Le Orme, Goblin or il Banco del Mutuo Soccorso but that blends vintage sounds with a contemporary musical landscape. The drawing on the cover is by Luca Di Pietro while in the booklet you can find some pictures that offer a glimpse of the music's inspiration..."777" is an excellent track that at times recalls Le Orme and, above all, Aliante. The title could be a reference to the model of a passenger plane. In fact, the 777 is the world's largest twin jet and the most-built wide-body airliner. Are you ready for a musical journey to new territories to discover? Well, get ready for take-off..."Gioia e risoluzione" (Joy and resolution) is another wonderful track beginning gently with a dreamy piano intro and then progressing through numerous changes in rhythm and mood. Although the title seems to paraphrase a well-known Area piece, the music is devoid of edgy experientialism and avant-garde overtones. Rather, it's in line with the previous track, cinematic and dreamy..."L'ineluttabile" (The inevitable) begins with a subdued rhythmic pattern that then intersects with restless melodic lines. The dark central section, with strong classical overtones and prominent piano, precedes a final part in crescendo..."Weltschmerz" opens with a melancholic atmosphere and the piano in the foreground. The title refers to a literary concept describing the feeling experienced by an individual who believes that reality can never satisfy the expectations of the mind, resulting in a mood of weariness or sadness about life arising from the acute awareness of evil and suffering. According to an interview with the band, "this piece was born to attempt to represent in music that malaise, so common today, caused by the dissatisfaction of living in a society where injustice and violence of every kind, both physical and mental, are everywhere. Those who identify with this malaise are unfortunately aware of their inadequacy in the face of the world's evils and suffer for it"..."Ripresa di coscienza" (Regaining consciousness) brings back a bit of positivity. After a dreamy start, the rhythm becomes more intense and fast-paced, almost as if to mark a reconciliation with life and reality...The following "Intro 442" is instead slower and darker, with the keyboards and piano weaving almost hypnotic textures that can bring to mind Goblin..."Lofoten" is calm and dreamy. In fact, the title refers to an archipelago and a traditional district in the county of Nordland, Norway. The Lofoten Islands boast unique landscapes, with towering mountains and peaks, open seas and sheltered bays, beaches and unspoiled lands. Landscapes that somehow inspired this piece..."Punto di fusione (Fusion point) is a beautiful track that recalls Banco del Mutuo Soccorso with some classical inspiration, a lot of energy and a remarkable melodic touch..."Il viaggio del Moro" (The Moro's voyage) closes the album with a cinematic and evocative atmosphere that recalls the opening track. The title seems to refer to the Moor of Venice, a famous regatta vessel, but this voyage proves far more adventurous and unpredictable than a simple sailing competition...On the whole, an excellent work!

items.body: Review by kev rowland — I must confess I was not a huge fan of the last album I heard from Solberg, 2024's 'The Congregation Acoustic', so when I realised he was releasing a second studio album I was not exactly jumping up and down with joy. This time around he decided to release an album which was highly symphonic, working with the Norwegian Radio Orchestra plus omusicians including drummer Keli Gu�j�nsson (Agent Fresco), violinist Chris Baum (Bent Knee), guitarist Pierre Danel (Novelists) & bassist Jed Lingat, as well as guitarists Ben Levin (ex-Bent Knee) & John Browne (Monuments).Conceptually this follows on from '16' which was where he revisited the death of his father and his past struggles with anxiety, as here he provides an intimate portrait of himself and how he views the world in 2026. Everything I felt was wrong with his last album is right here, with the orchestra very much at the heart of the proceedings and the rock fitting in seamlessly, and then over the top are his incredible vocals. He is undoubtedly one of the finest singers in the industry and here he uses his complete range, whether that is going up the range into falsetto with no hint of strain or providing vocal gymnastics which makes one wonder where he is going next.This is very different indeed to "just" a singer performing with accompaniment, but being instead being very much part of the band himself, and the only other person I can think of who has really achieved this is Ian Gillan more than 50 years ago when he used his voice as an incredible instrument when he was at the height of his powers. This is an album where the listener not only enjoys the highly cinematic and emotional approach, but also in somewhat in awe of what Solberg can do. It is very much a singer's album, but this time it works incredibly well, and it is impossible to imagine this release without everything which is going on vocally. The result is something which feels more like opera, or a stage show, than an album with the listener being taken deep inside in a way which is quite incredible.

The name Nashwa is Arabic for euphoria, ecstasy or trance, inviting us for a transcendental musical experience. items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — Despite being impressively technical and complex, Between the Buried and Me's 'Alaska' relies alittle too much on the neurotic explosion of aggressive riffs and stampeding time signatures, whichrenders the band's third full-length studio album somewhat strenuous and puzzling. As one of themasters of Crimson-esque riffs, this BTBAM release is actually replete with great ideas, complexarrangements, and some downright mad instrumental sections. Yet despite all of these interestingfeatures, 'Alaska' suffers from an impending technicality that erases the distinction of theindividual contributions of the five band members, which is a pity knowing that these are some ofthe most technically gifted musicians of the 2000s progressive metalcore scene. Relentless andobscure, this release captures an interesting transitional period for BTBAM, being the first onewith what many would consider the classic lineup of Tommy Giles Rogers, Paul Waggoner, and then-newcomers Dan Briggs (bass), Dusty Waring (guitars), and Blake Richardson (drums), who would go onto play together until Waring's 2023 departure.Knowing how the band's sound would develop, I can hear many exemplary motives and stylistic quirkson 'Alaska', but I can also imagine someone who is just getting into the band could easily bedisappointed by this album. The blatant aggression that the band is capable of achieving intertwinesin a peculiar way with the extreme speed and incessant technicality of their playing, which providesfor an unusual sonic experience, albeit not a dramatically enjoyable one. This is precisely why Ithink 'Alaska' remains a fav-favorite, nevertheless. It contains several excellent tracks, some ofwhich are remarkable examples of BTBAM's unmistakable songwriting, like the frantic opener 'AllBodies' or the proggy mathcore number 'Selkies: The Endless Obsession', which many fans see as a keyalbum track. Other stellar songs here include the lengthier pieces 'Roboturner' and 'BackwardsMarathon', which for me exemplify brilliantly the whole point of the band's deviant style. Thisalbum is a great listen if you are looking for extremely aggressive and overly technical progressivemetal, and while it does contain many interesting moments, the majority of the band's later albumsare undoubtedly superior to 'Alaska'.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑属于技术极端前卫金属风格，是乐队阵容调整后过渡阶段的作品。音乐以复杂的编曲、快速变换的节拍和极具攻击性的吉他 riff 为特点，融合了前卫金属核与数学核元素。作品整体听感密集且晦涩，技术表现力突出，但有时会因过度复杂而削弱成员间的辨识度。专辑中包含多首长篇曲目，展现了乐队标志性的偏离式创作风格，如《Selkies: The Endless Obsession》等曲目。虽然该作在乐迷中具有一定代表性，但从整体听感来看，其后的作品在成熟度上更胜一筹。

items.body: Review by Aussie-Byrd-Brother — A short-lived one-and-done band formed in Karlsruhe, Germany, Poseidon's sole release `Found My Way' dropped in 1975, and the group sure displayed a split personality on it! Too tidy to be considered `Krautrock', too tune-based to be proper psychedelic/space-rock, Poseidon sung in softly accented English and took the song-focused parts of fellow German bands like Jane, Walpurgis, Kin Ping Meh, Wallenstein and Satin Whale, and probably veered closest to the crossover approach of Swiss psych-rockers Krokodil.The ringing acoustic guitars of instantly inviting opener `The Trip' accompanies Horst Meinzer's charismatic rasp, the softly melancholic ballad joyfully lifting in tempo around sparkling electric piano and a strident beat. The mellow but charmingly messy `Swimming Against The Stream' opens as a lethargic acid-rock ballad with swirling effects and humming Hammond organ before frantic Moog twirls and ragged guitar soloing completely swarm the tune! Sweetly murmuring bass slides behind reflective rocker `How Heavy The Days' that holds a lyric that moves between sad and hopeful, aptly conveyed by some ragged electric guitar fire and a spirited duel of Moog and Hammond organ.On the flip-side, there's sun-kissed jangling guitar licks and peppy percussion throughout `Cold Farmer', and group harmonies, while a little messy, convey sincerity. Instrumental `Surprise' is just that, a welcome sprint around everything from wavering synths atmospheres, mystical ambient chimes, funky bass workouts and grandiose Floydian guitar reaches. The peppy title-track closer has all the musicians delivering little standout moments, and an ambitious extended instrumental middle of droning electronics behind mysterious electric guitar musings brings the band the closest to the cosmic contemplations of fellow German groups Eloy and Novalis...but what a shame it all simply ends on an uninspired fade-out mid-vocal!While some parts of the album are a little shambolic and a few transitions a tad forced, `Found my Way' is melodic with very colourful, lively and energetic playing, gentle fuzzy edges, and the whole set hums with good intentions, positivity and warmth. If you don't go into this expecting a full-blown prog blow-out, it's a well-deserved three and a half stars.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由德国乐队波塞冬于1975年发行，风格介于迷幻摇滚与太空摇滚之间。作品以歌曲创作为核心，融合了柔和的原声吉他、哈蒙德风琴、穆格合成器以及略带粗糙质感的吉他独奏。音乐情绪在忧郁与积极之间切换，既有抒情慢板，也包含节奏明快的器乐段落。整体演奏充满活力与温暖感，带有德国同代乐队的一些特征，但并未进行深度的前卫或实验性探索。专辑结构偏向传统摇滚编排，部分过渡略显生硬，结尾处理较为平淡。

items.body: Aleesha Dibbs has spent enough time inside other people’s music to know the difference between presence and ornament. As a keys player, vocalist, and session musician, she has moved through large stages and strange rooms alike, working with Karen O, Angus & Julia Stone, Lisa Mitchell, MT Warning, Prudence, Lorelei, All Sparks Burn Out, and her own earlier projects Dive Bell and Double Vision. On Big Mood, her debut solo album, that accumulated fluency becomes a private language, one built from post-punk pressure, alternative-pop immediacy, and the kind of low-lit physicality that suggests Fontaines D.C., Kim Gordon, and Warpaint passing through the same locked corridor without agreeing on the exit. The first single, Waiting Game, sets the tone with unusual patience, taking an existential premise and keeping it close to the body: postponement, delayed consequence, the strange private arithmetic of choosing one door while imagining the life behind another. Dibbs sings as though she is measuring the distance between instinct and action, holding herself in the charged interval before a decision hardens into fate. The track gathers force by degrees, refusing any cheap revelation; its tension comes from pressure carefully held, from the sense that hesitation can become its own kind of habitat. Around her, the guitars scrape and flare, bringing to mind the slackened bite of Liz Phair, the bruised melodic force of The Breeders, and the serrated pop logic of Pixies. Dibbs bends those references toward her own temperament, allowing the song’s hook to feel less like a slogan than a communal exhale, a chant formed at the edge of recognition. Waiting Game treats pause as an active state, full of consequence, appetite, and risk. The song understands that waiting can be a form of paralysis, but also a form of preparation: the breath before speech, the hand before the handle, the life one imagines before stepping into the one that remains. That credo could sound inflated in lesser hands. Dibbs makes it lived-in, tensile, and exact. Waiting Game is the sound of an artist ready to step into the limelight. Listen below, and order the single here. Waiting Game by Aleesha Dibbs Across Big Mood, Dibbs writes against emotional compression, against the tidy self one is expected to maintain while screens multiply, attention fragments, and feeling becomes another inconvenience to be managed. The record’s title has a wry bluntness, yet the songs are finely calibrated, turning large states of mind into taut arrangements and charged vocal lines. Produced, engineered, and mixed over three years by longtime collaborator Tom Crandles, whose credits include Au.Ra, Prudence, and DMA’s, the album carries the mark of careful construction without losing its nerve. The mastering, completed at Black Knoll Studios in New York City, gives the record a clean edge that suits its conflict between control and release. Dibbs’s own description remains the best key to the album’s ethic: “For the most part, Big Mood is about fighting back,” she says. “It’s about saying, unapologetically, yes to big feelings. It’s about uncovering and embracing self-agency, taking up as much or as little space as you need. And ultimately, it’s about remembering we’re human, submitting to whatever needs to pass through, without guilt and without apology.” Follow Aleesha Dibbs: Facebook Instagram Spotify Bandcamp LinkTree The post Sydney’s Aleesha Dibbs Asks Existential Questions With “Waiting Game,” The First Single From Forthcoming Album “Big Mood” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: "The jazz bandstand is where true democracy lives," the great saxophonist and composer Jimmy Heath told a young Helen Sung. "Everyone must understand their role and come prepared by doing the hard work of study and practice," he said. "Each person will get to say their piece, but it is in the act of integrating as a band that the musicians ultimately create something bigger, richer, and deeper." Oracles launches into a time and place where divisions are deep and democracy is under attack, which makes it a perfect moment to reflect on and embrace Heath's view. As her first big-band offering, the album is Sung's response—to Heath and Clark Terry, Ron Carter, Wayne Shorter, Barry Harris, Kenny Barron, Herbie Hancock, and Sir Roland Hanna—which, as she put it, "expresses my deep gratitude and is a tribute to the masters who made room for me and entrusted me with a tradition they helped build." Her compositions affirm lessons she has learned and values she has internalized. In "A Little Bird Watchin' (for Jimmy Heath)," the ensemble leads the way. What begins with one voice (Nicole Glover's tenor saxophone) quickly becomes lively counterpoint as independent lines are layered in, followed by full-voiced harmonious homophony. Improvisation is the order of the day, with Vicente Archer's bass, Sung's piano, and Adam Cruz's drums coming to the fore as textures and tempos shift. Soloists dominate. There is plenty of composition, but it serves and is led by individual voices (those of "the people," to use Heath's metaphor). Taking Ron Carter's advice to heart, that "in order to find your voice in this music, you have to write your own music," she uses material by her mentors as jumping-off points for creations that are very much her own. Terry's "Samba da Gumz" (track 2) becomes a prelude to her "Positively C.T." (track 3), which highlights her trumpets (Mike Rodriguez, Tatum Greenblatt, Alex Norris, Nathaniel Williford). And Shorter's gorgeous "Diana" (track 4), which Shorter so memorably offered in his 1974 collaboration with Milton Nascimento (Native Dancer, Columbia), here becomes a dreamy prelude for soprano sax (John Ellis) and Fender Rhodes, leading to Sung's quixotic "Wayne's World" (track 5). Sung's "Mr. Virtuoso" (track 6), written for Carter, opens with bass, piano, and drums in an out-of-time misterioso before she employs the full range of the ensemble, from flutes on top to the lower realms of her reed and brass sections. She plumbs the depths with solos from Andrew Gutauskas' baritone saxophone and Gina Benalcázar López's bass trombone then uses Carter's own "R.J." as a postlude, picking up the tempo and again centering on the rhythm section. Sung followed Hanna's counsel to "not forget her classical roots" in composing Pianism, a piano concerto in tribute to Harris, Barron, and Hancock. The first movement, "I: Barry Harris," opens with a non-blues pentatonic passage in parallel harmony that is gradually reshaped metrically against a changing set of backdrops, finally settling—two minutes into the performance—into a bop melodic, rhythmic, and harmonic milieu reflective of Harris' position as "keeper of Bud Powell's legacy and the bebop flame." The timbres soften in the second movement, "II: Kenny Barron," which honors the "modern master of melody" with Rhodes, flute, and muted trumpet lines that sail on a cool groove that navigates swing and straight eighths. "III: Herbie Hancock," comes on strong with percussion hits and horns in a pentatonic canon that recalls the concerto's opening while heralding a funkier feel with a finely calibrated 16th-note subdivision and blues mode in its melodic backbone. In keeping with her view of Hancock as "transcendence personified," Sung closes the concerto with a finale that aligns conceptually with aesthetic and formal norms of classical composition. She reminds us who and what we have heard in earlier movements, recapping themes, playing with and intertwining elements, transcending stylistic boundaries to create a work that—while it respects the "without you, no me" jazz principle—is undeniably, joyfully original.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是海伦·桑的首张大乐队爵士作品，以向吉米·希斯、罗恩·卡特等爵士大师致敬为核心主题。音乐在大型乐团的编制下展开，注重个体即兴表达与整体合奏的平衡，编曲融合了复调对位与和声织体。作品将导师的经典曲目作为引子，发展出具有个人风格的创作段落，其中还融入了钢琴协奏曲形式的尝试，结合了古典音乐背景与爵士语汇，整体风格偏向学院派与主流大乐队传统的结合。

items.body: Lords of Acid newest single”El Mundo Está Loco” is out today, June 12, 2026 through Metropolis Records. The single features the New York City duo Tony & The Kiki and is the third Lords of Acid single of 2026. It is available to stream and through the band’s Bandcamp page. The title translates as “the world is crazy”. The track combines electronic beats and Latin-inspired hooks with a vocal exchange between Lords of Acid and Tony & The Kiki. Metropolis Records describes “El Mundo Está Loco” as “a dance floor anthem for a world that seems to be getting crazier by the day”. Tony & The Kiki are a New York glam-rock duo formed in 2021 by vocalist Anthony Alfaro and keyboardist Rodney Bush. The pair appeared as one of the guest acts on the recently completed “Cheeky Freaky Tour” of the United States with Lords of Acid. “El Mundo Está Loco” is a digital single; no physical format has been announced. El Mundo Está Loco by Lords of Acid feat. Tony & The Kiki “El Mundo Está Loco” follows the 2026 singles “Karaoke Superstar” and “Dream Boy”. Side-Line already covered “Karaoke Superstar”, a collaboration with vocalist and DJ Princess Superstar. “Dream Boy” features Carla Harvey, the group’s current vocalist. All three songs are set to appear on a seventh Lords of Acid studio album due in late 2026, first reported by Side-Line alongside the band’s “Cheeky Freaky” US tour. The label states the album will feature further guest vocalists alongside Harvey. About Lords of Acid Lords of Acid formed in Antwerp, Belgium in 1988 around producer Praga Khan (Maurice Engelen). The group combined techno, acid house, New Beat and industrial elements with lyrics centred on sexuality, drug culture and hedonism. They debuted with the single “I Sit On Acid”, and their first album “Lust” followed in 1991. Subsequent releases placed the group on the Billboard dance and alternative charts, and the band has maintained a long-running international touring schedule. The current line-up includes vocalist Carla Harvey, formerly of Butcher Babies, whom is the band’s new singer since January 2025. “El Mundo Está Loco” continues the run of 2026 singles leading toward the group’s seventh studio album.
items._cn_summary: 工业电子乐队Lords of Acid于2026年6月发布新单曲《El Mundo Está Loco》，由纽约双人组合Tony & The Kiki参与客座演唱。作品融合电子节拍与拉丁风格旋律，围绕“世界疯狂”的主题展开人声对唱，被厂牌定位为舞池风格作品。该曲是乐队2026年第三支单曲，前作包括与Princess Superstar及现任主唱Carla Harvey的合作曲目。三首作品均将收录于乐队年内推出的第七张录音室专辑。乐队自1988年成立，风格涵盖酸性浩室、新节拍与工业元素，题材多涉及享乐主义与亚文化。

items.body: Stolen, the post-punk/electronic band from Chengdu, China, play two London shows at The George Tavern on July 12 and 13, 2026. The concerts are the final stop of the band’s current tour. The two July dates follow the band’s previous London appearance at Scala on October 6, 2024, which was part of their “I Generated” UK and European tour. You can order your tickets right here. “Cacophonic Symphony” is the band’s latest studio album. The nine-track record, which includes the songs “Electric Baby”, “Bouquet”, “Polythene Town” and “Dress Code”, appeared in April 2026 as a self-released album. Cacophonic Symphony by STOLEN About Stolen Stolen formed in Chengdu, in China’s Sichuan province; and more precisely at the Sichuan Conservatory of Music in 2009. The line-up consists of Liang Yi (vocals), FangDe (guitar), JunYang (bass), YuFeng (drums) and Duan Xuan (keyboards), joined since 2012 by French visual artist Formol, who handles the band’s live visuals. After the EP “Strange Old-fashioned Entertainment” (2013) and the album “Loop” (2015, D Force Records), the band began working with Berlin-based producer Mark Reeder, who produced their 2017 self-titled EP. Reeder, together with Micha Adam, also produced the album “Fragment”, released on October 26, 2018 through Reeder’s reactivated MFS label. The Reeder connection led to the band opening for New Order on a run of European dates in October 2019, including shows in Berlin and Paris. The album “Eroded Creation” followed on December 19, 2022, and the EP “I Generated” in September 2024, supported by a UK and European tour that year. “Cacophonic Symphony”, released in April 2026, is the band’s most recent album, and the July dates at The George Tavern are the band’s first announced London shows since its release. Below is the love release “Dance Tunnel 26′ Long Mix (live)” on which the band deconstructed and rearranged several of the band’s classic works, adapting them to their current sound. Tracks included are “Electric Baby”, “Space Intruders”, “Pay”, “AI Arena”, “Copy Shop”, “Why We Choose To Die In Berlin” and “Overfeed”. The whole comes as a 26+ minute long track. items._cn_summary: 这是一篇关于成都后朋克与电子乐队Stolen的演出新闻稿。乐队融合后朋克、电子声响与实验元素，风格接近暗潮与工业电子的跨界方向。最新专辑《Cacophonic Symphony》为自主发行，包含九首作品，延续其冷峻的电子摇滚路线。乐队与柏林制作人合作，曾担任New Order巡演嘉宾，具有一定的国际地下音乐场景定位。文中提供的音频示例为长达二十六分钟的现场混音，对过往作品进行了解构与重组，体现出一定的实验编排思路。整体内容以巡演信息与乐队历程为主，未涉及深入的创作分析。

items.body: AD Ozium, the Washington, D.C. project led by Jeremy Moore, released the album “In the Style of Dead Sparrows” offering a mix of drone, noise and dark ambient. The release is available through the project’s Bandcamp page. On this new release Moore weaves folk, jazz and no wave into a continuous, structure-less form. The album is available via the project’s Bandcamp page. The album follows “If Membership Is Slumber”, a two-track release that pairs the vocal piece “Terrorgramophone” with the instrumental “Lifespring”. In The Style Of Dead Sparrows by AD Ozium About AD Ozium AD Ozium is a Washington, D.C.-based project by Jeremy Moore. The project combines folk, jazz, no wave, dark ambient and noise rock elements with abrasive textures, fractured rhythms, drones, loops and unstable guitar passages. Moore handles guitars, synthesis, drones, loops and noise, with vocals also credited on the earlier release “If Membership Is Slumber”. The project appeared publicly in 2026 through Saccharine Underground, the Washington, D.C. musical collective, artist network and non-profit label connected to Moore’s wider body of work. At Side-Line we previously covered Moore’s related projects in Zabus release second album in three months: “The Future of Death” – Out now and Bell Barrow drops debut LP “CoreCore Pulp” – Out now. The first AD Ozium release, “If Membership Is Slumber”, was issued on May 19, 2026. The two-track release contains “Terrorgramophone” and “Lifespring”. The material was recorded between January and March 2026 at The Prisoner’s Cinema in Washington, D.C., engineered by Andy Baldwin at Metropolis Studios in April 2026 and produced by Moore. The project’s next release, “In the Style of Dead Sparrows”, followed on June 9, 2026. The 10-track digital album includes “Lifespring”, “Tender Loving Seed”, “Whore of Sound”, “Music From The Opfer’s Box”, “Faith Is A Hole”, “Portents of The Terminal Mind”, “The Nazarene Distortion”, “Death Valley Superbloom”, “Throne Verse” and “A Practical Act of Prowess”. This album was recorded between January and February 2026 at The Prisoner’s Cinema in Washington, D.C. as well, and was engineered by Andy Baldwin at Metropolis Studios in May 2026 and produced by Moore. Moore also created the cover concept and design. AD Ozium sits close to his more textural and unstable work. Zabus used progressive post-punk, proto-goth and electronic percussion structures, while his other project Bell Barrow moved into instrumental noise, power electronics, free jazz psychedelia and avant-garde black metal. “In the Style of Dead Sparrows” is available as a digital album through AD Ozium’s Bandcamp page.
items._cn_summary: AD Ozium 是来自美国华盛顿特区的音乐项目，由杰里米·摩尔主导。新专辑《In the Style of Dead Sparrows》融合了民谣、爵士、无浪潮、暗潮氛围与噪音摇滚元素，以无序结构串联，包含十首曲目。作品运用粗粝质感、断裂节奏、无人机音墙、循环采样与不稳定吉他段落，声响风格偏向实验性与不稳定性。录音于华盛顿特区的 The Prisoner’s Cinema 完成，后期由安迪·鲍德温在 Metropolis 工作室处理，整体定位属于小众地下实验场景，与作者其他侧重后朋克、噪音与自由爵士的项目形成风格互补。

items.body: London dark electronic duo Palindrones have released a new single, “The Blood Moon“, it’s available now on Bandcamp. The track arrives with an accompanying music video. Palindrones described “The Blood Moon” as “a dark, hypnotic journey through the tides, storms, sin and submission,” adding that the single is “a tale of the cycles of destruction, renewal and the ancient currents that flow beneath human experience.” The band furthermore says that “like the celestial body that gives the song its name, it pulls listeners into a world where scars become constellations, rivers run red, and every ending delivers the seed of creation.” Here is the music video for “The Blood Moon”. About Palindrones Palindrones is a dark electronic duo from South London, who describe their sound as “dreamy Industrial Synthpop” with “pounding rhythms, haunting, evocative vocals and esoteric ambiance.” The project consists of Karen and Jamie. Side-Line first covered the duo in April 2023, when it premiered the ‘Samadhi’ single and video from its then-upcoming second album, “Chapter One: With Fearful Velocity.” In March 2025, the duo returned with the ‘Animus’ single and video. The act has also worked with the goth band Hurtsfall, which issued a Palindrones remix of its track “Adore Me” as a World Goth Day free download. “The Blood Moon,” released on June 12, 2026, is the duo’s latest single.

items.body: (Photo via GRIT PHOTOZINE) Boy Harsher, the American darkwave duo, have announced “The Heartbreak Tour”, a North American run that opens on June 26, 2026 in San Francisco and resumes for a main leg from September 25 to November 5, 2026 across the United States and Canada. Tickets go on sale on June 12, 2026 at 10 a.m. local time. The Heartbreak Tour is the duo’s first extensive North American headlining run since the 2022 touring for their short film and soundtrack “The Runner”. Jae Matthews and Augustus Muller open on June 26 at 1015 Folsom in San Francisco, then begin the main leg on September 25 at Basilica Hudson in Hudson, New York. The routing moves through Boston, Montreal, Toronto, Detroit, Chicago, Minneapolis, Denver, Portland, Seattle, Vancouver, Oakland, Los Angeles, Del Mar, Las Vegas, Phoenix, Fort Worth, New Orleans, Atlanta, Asheville, Washington, Philadelphia and Queens, where it closes on November 5 at Knockdown Center. The schedule includes two-night stands at Chicago’s Metro, Portland’s Revolution Hall and Seattle’s The Showbox. Boy Harsher tour dates 2026 Support on select dates comes from Choir Boy, Evanora Unlimited, True Blue and Kassie Krut. The October 24 date in Fort Worth is part of Sick New World – DFW. June 26 – San Francisco, CA – 1015 Folsom September 25 – Hudson, NY – Basilica Hudson September 27 – Boston, MA – Royale September 29 – Montreal, QC – MTELUS September 30 – Toronto, ON – Danforth Music Hall October 1 – Detroit, MI – Majestic Theatre October 2 – Chicago, IL – Metro October 3 – Chicago, IL – Metro October 4 – Minneapolis, MN – Varsity Theater October 6 – Denver, CO – Summit October 9 – Portland, OR – Revolution Hall October 10 – Portland, OR – Revolution Hall October 11 – Seattle, WA – The Showbox October 12 – Seattle, WA – The Showbox October 13 – Vancouver, BC – The Pearl October 15 – Oakland, CA – Fox Theater October 16 – Los Angeles, CA – Hollywood Palladium October 17 – Del Mar, CA – The Sound October 20 – Las Vegas, NV – House of Blues October 21 – Phoenix, AZ – The Van Buren October 24 – Fort Worth, TX – Sick New World – DFW October 26 – New Orleans, LA – Republic NOLA October 27 – Atlanta, GA – Variety Playhouse October 28 – Asheville, NC – The Orange Peel October 30 – Washington, DC – The Howard Theatre October 31 – Philadelphia, PA – Franklin Music Hall (Making Time Pure Halloween) November 5 – Queens, NY – Knockdown Center Tickets go on sale on June 12, 2026 at 10 a.m. local time. Boy Harsher have not announced European dates as part of this run. About Boy Harsher Boy Harsher formed in 2014 in Savannah, Georgia, where vocalist Jae Matthews and producer Augustus Muller met in film school. The pair first worked together as Teen Dreamz in 2013, mixing Matthews’s spoken word with Muller’s electronics, before renaming the project Boy Harsher and releasing the home-recorded EP “Lesser Man” the same year. They later relocated to Northampton, Massachusetts. The duo released their debut album “Yr Body Is Nothing” in 2016 through DKA Records, followed by the “Country Girl” EP in 2017. In 2018 they set up their own label, Nude Club, and reissued earlier material. Their second studio album, Boy Harsher – Careful (CD Album – Nude Club Records), arrived on February 1, 2019, with the remix set “Careful Remixes, etc.” issued the same year. In January 2022 Matthews and Muller released their directorial debut, the short film “The Runner”, with an accompanying soundtrack, followed with festival appearances including Primavera Sound, Roadburn and Coachella. In November 2024 the duo featured on Pet Shop Boys’ double A-side single “New London Boy / All The Young Dudes”, while Muller continued his Safe Mind project with Cooper B. Handy. The Heartbreak Tour is the duo’s first extended North American headlining run since the 2022 cycle around “The Runner”, returning Boy Harsher to the stage with shows from June through November 2026.

items.body: Today the German EBM and electro duo Digital Factor have officially released their new album “0.8” through the Belgian label Alfa Matrix. The twelve-track record arrives on CD (available via Alfa Matrix), and in digital formats. It follows the band’s 2021 album “A Chemical Process” and the 2023 charity album “G.B.A. – General Behavior Abrogate“. The band now is a duo with Mike Langer and permanent new member Gwendolyn Gaffa who already contributed on the EP “They Will Forget You (When You Die)” and on the 2023 charity single “I Am What I Am“, released as a free download. We published a full interview with Digital factor two days ago. ‘0.8’ tracklist, guests and 1980s concept The album contains twelve tracks and two guest features. Franziska Haucke appears on “Never”, and Marie-Luis Kiessling features on “We Are Blind”. The record is a return to the band’s formative era, diving deep into the musical and cultural DNA of the 1980s. The first single “They Will Forget You (When You Die)” for instance already carries a nod to Depeche Mode’s “People Are People”, while the album track “Time” is presented as a homage to Kraftwerk. Langer also used a special production method for “0.8”. He deliberately stepped away from modern production perfection, using stripped-down setups and monophonic synths to recreate the raw textures and subtle imperfections of early electronic music. Good to know, “Feel To Little” uses speech fragments from Charlie Chaplin films, while “Never” is set to a James Bond-style atmosphere. 0.8 by DIGITAL FACTOR About Digital Factor The band formed in 1993 in Altenburg, Germany. The founding lineup consisted of Torsten Heise, Mike Langer and Tino Schmidt. The project first brought a mix of EBM and electro, later adding techno, synth-pop and crossover elements,. They played early live support for acts such as Placebo Effect and X Marks the Pedwalk. The band’s first release was the 1994 EP “F.A.L.L.I.N.G.- Down” on Hard Records. A move to Hyperium and Hypnobeat followed, bringing the debut album “Relationchips” in 1995 and the conceptual second album “On Demand” in 1996. Relationchips (Remastered) by DIGITAL FACTOR Falling Down (Remastered) EP by DIGITAL FACTOR Further releases included “De Facto” and “Countercheck” in 1997 and “Over One Million Times” in 1999, then “One More Piece” in 2006, “Look Back To Go Forward” in 2009 and “Trialog” in 2011. Tino Schmidt left the band in its earlier years, and in 2010 Torsten Heise left and was replaced by Leo von Leibnitz. On Demand (Remastered) by DIGITAL FACTOR The band joined Alfa Matrix in 2020 and released the single and video ‘Come With Me’ in October of the same year. Come With Me EP by DIGITAL FACTOR The album “A Chemical Process” arrived in 2021, alongside remastered reissues of the back catalogue. The EP “What?” followed in 2022, and 2023 brought the charity single “I Am What I Am“, the “Ouvre” EP and the charity album “G.B.A. – General Behavior Abrogate“. items.body: In an era when contemporary classical music often gravitates toward conceptual complexity, sonic experimentation, or large-scale ambition, Canadian composer Joel Toews takes a markedly different path with We Remember Moments. This deeply personal collection of chamber and piano works is rooted not in grand narratives but in fragments of lived experience—the fleeting, emotionally charged moments that linger long after the details have faded. The album takes its inspiration from a quotation by Cesare Pavese: “We do not remember days, we remember moments.” That idea serves as both philosophical framework and compositional method. As Toews explains in the accompanying booklet, these pieces are not intended as detailed recollections of specific events but rather as musical manifestations of emotional memories—snapshots of people, places, and experiences that continue to shape us long after they have passed.   What immediately stands out throughout the album is the composer’s commitment to sincerity. The melodic language is direct, the harmonic vocabulary largely accessible, and the formal structures uncomplicated. Yet this simplicity is entirely intentional. Rather than seeking to impress through technical display, Toews embraces restraint, allowing melody and atmosphere to carry the emotional weight. The result is music that feels intimate and unguarded, inviting listeners into a private world while leaving ample space for their own memories to resonate within it.   The opening track, “Four Thousand and One,” sets the tone beautifully. Named after the first apartment Toews shared with his partner in Toronto, the piece reflects a period marked by new beginnings, personal growth, and a series of life-defining firsts. Its gentle piano writing possesses an almost diary-like quality, balancing optimism with reflection. The music unfolds naturally, as though remembering rather than narrating, establishing the album’s central theme from its very first phrases.   One of the album’s most evocative moments arrives with “Evergreen.” Inspired by the forests of the Canadian wilderness, the piece pairs piano with harp, performed by Jacqueline Goring. This unusual combination proves remarkably effective. Toews associates the harp with the deep green hues of evergreen forests, and the instrument’s shimmering textures create an atmosphere that feels simultaneously expansive and intimate. Rather than functioning as program music, the piece captures the emotional essence of nature—the sense of wonder, solitude, and contemplation that landscapes can inspire.   “January (of 2020)” occupies a particularly compelling place within the collection. Originating from a compositional exercise in which Toews committed himself to writing at least two measures of music every day for a month, the work gained unexpected significance in retrospect. Written just weeks before the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, it now represents a final glimpse of normalcy before a period of unprecedented global uncertainty. The music’s calm, measured character acquires an almost poignant quality when viewed through that historical lens, becoming a reminder of how little we often know about the changes awaiting us.  The emotional center of the album may well be “Prairie Skies,” dedicated to the composer’s late grandmother, Phyllis Rempel. Drawing on childhood memories of rural Alberta—tractor rides, endless fields, and vast prairie horizons—the piece radiates warmth and affection. Particularly touching is the incorporation of the hymn How Great Thou Art near the conclusion, a tribute to his grandmother’s faith that never feels imposed or sentimental. Instead, it emerges organically from the musical narrative, transforming personal remembrance into something universally recognizable.   If Prairie Skies looks back through the lens of family, “August (of 2006)” revisits the freedom of adolescence. Inspired by memories of being twelve years old and discovering independence through endless bicycle rides and childhood exploration, the piece channels nostalgia without becoming trapped by it. Folk influences emerge through the interplay of violin and guitar, lending the music a buoyant energy and rustic charm. The result is one of the album’s most vividly cinematic moments, rich with movement and youthful possibility.   The album’s most distinctive timbral departure comes with “Solace.” Built around a trumpet melody that first appeared as a voice memo recorded during a solitary walk, the work embodies the creative process itself: an idea caught in passing and later transformed into something fully realized. Trumpeter Matt Smith delivers the melody with warmth and clarity, bringing a spacious, almost pastoral quality to the music. The piece underscores one of the album’s recurring themes—that moments of solitude often become fertile ground for both memory and creativity.   The collection concludes with “Stephanie’s Theme,” a solo piano work dedicated to one of Toews’ closest friends and longtime supporters. Originally written years earlier and later performed by the composer at her wedding, the piece serves as a fitting finale. After the varied instrumental colours explored throughout the album, the return to solo piano feels like a homecoming. The music is elegant, lyrical, and deeply personal, bringing the album full circle.   Equally deserving of praise is the ensemble of collaborators who help bring these memories to life. Harpist Jacqueline Goring, violinist William Lamereaux, guitarist Jess Lajner, and trumpeter Matt Smith each contribute performances marked by sensitivity and restraint. Their playing never seeks the spotlight; instead, it reinforces the album’s central commitment to emotional authenticity. The production, mixed by Toews and mastered by Reuben Ghose, complements this aesthetic perfectly, favouring warmth and clarity over excessive polish.   What makes We Remember Moments ultimately compelling is not its ambition to redefine contemporary classical music, but its confidence in embracing vulnerability. Toews understands that some of the most meaningful artistic experiences arise not from complexity but from recognition—from hearing something that mirrors our own inner lives. These compositions may originate in deeply personal memories, yet they consistently transcend autobiography, inviting listeners to revisit their own moments worth remembering. In doing so, We Remember Moments becomes more than a collection of compositions. It becomes a quiet reflection on memory itself: imperfect, selective, fragile, and profoundly human. discover Joel’s music here: The post Echoes Between the Notes: Joel Toews’ Meditation on Memory in We Remember Moments first appeared on Modern Classical Music.

items.body: Top Picks Genghis Tron – Signal Fire (posty-matchore, cybergrind?) There are those around here who revere it, but for me, the resurrection of progressive cybergrind pioneers Genghis Tron as a boring, trendy dream-pop band, with 2021's Dream Weapon, is one of the bigger musical let-downs of recent memory. Signal Fire, on the other hand, perfectly spits the difference, bringing back a lot more of the band's progressive tendencies, alongside some harsher vocals and an alternative-industrial elements, reminiscent of Health or even Filter in their more 90s-coded moments. It's a balanced approach that keeps the best of what Genghis Tron learned on Dream Weapon, while also retaining a lot of what made them so special in the first place. and—from the few quick listens I've managed to give it today—I'd say it's rather superb. items.body: British band Aiming released a four-track EP last year on Blackjack Illuminist Records and returns this year with a new release featuring another four tracks. Aiming continues to draw on a range of influences, blending Shoegaze with touches of Dream-Pop. More than ever, the fuzzy guitar work creates a distinctive atmosphere that permeates all the songs. At times, especially when paired with the female vocals, it evokes a sense of melancholy. Overall, the music remains subdued and dreamy, and Aiming delivers four enjoyable tracks, with the opening song standing out as the clear highlight. (Rating:7½). Listen to “Our Voices At The Bottom Of The Ocean”: https://blackjackilluministrecords.bandcamp.com/track/our-voices-at-the-bottom-of-the-ocean

This is a unique 7" test pressing of Gilbert Shelton and his band performing "Southern Stock Car Race" and "If I Was A Hell's Angel". It is the only one in existence. This important piece of Underground history is hand labeled by Shelton, and would be a significant addition to any serious Underground collection! This serious piece of underground history was contained for decades in William Helmer's infamous footlocker cache. You can try, but we guarantee that you will never find another example like this. Be the first person to listen to this record since the mid Sixties!From Austin Texas, Gilbert Shelton was of course the reknowned Wonder Wart-Hog comics artist, later responsible for the ubiqutous Furry Freak Brothers empire. This appears to be his sole recording, on which he was backed by members of The Conqueroo and Tom Bright, who later played with Black Swan. You can also find Hell's Angel on Collectables' '69 Love-In (CD)."I issued a 45 featuring IF I WAS A HELL'S ANGEL, but I do not recall the title on the other side but it may have been the one featured here. This must have been issued by Gilbert Shelton himself." -Bernard Stollman

多様性のあるレパートリーの構築を目指して、日本と英国を拠点に活動。東京藝術大学音楽学部附属音楽高等学校を経て同大学音楽学部器楽科卒業、同声会賞を受賞。英国王立音楽院修... 詳しく見る 音楽の友 編集部 月刊誌 1941年12月創刊。音楽之友社の看板雑誌「音楽の友」を毎月刊行しています。“音楽の深層を知り、音楽家の本音を聞く”がモットー。今月号のコンテンツはこちらバックナンバ... 詳しく見る 2026年5月の英国ロイヤル・オペラ・ハウスは、サン=サーンス《サムソンとデリラ》（『音楽の友』2026年7月号にてレポート）とブリテン《ピーター・グライムズ》を交互に上演し大賑わいであったが、地下にあるリンブリー・シアターでは若手育成プログラム「ジェット・パーカー・アーティスト」による意欲的な公演が行われた。約400席の劇場は、小さいながらも本格的なシアターになっていて、新星のデビューや新作上演などに活用されている。 5月1日から9日に上演された『Tales of Love and Loss』は、女性作曲家作品のトリプル・ビル（一つの公演の中で異なる三つの短い作品をまとめて上演するプログラム形式）で、エリザベス・マコンキー（1907-94）《The Departure》、シャーロット・ブレイ（1982年生まれ）《Making Arrangements》、そしてエレーナ・ランゲル（1974年生まれ）《Four Sisters》の3演目で構成。音楽監督はタリア・スターン、指揮はペギー・ウー、そして歌手は「ジェット・パーカー・アーティスト」の面々が務める。管弦楽はブリテン・シンフォニアが担当。筆者は千秋楽を聴いた。 マコンキーは、生前英国王室から叙勲された実力派の作曲家である。オペラを6作書いたが、《The Departure》は小編成であるのが特徴。舞台に出てくる歌手は二人きり、ただしバンダ（小規模アンサンブル）でのコーラスがあり、雰囲気は満点だ。音楽の構成としては、短いながらクラシカルな作り。舞台は妻が自身の死に気づかず部屋で夫を待つシーンから始まり、本人と共に観客も徐々に彼女が死んでいることを悟るサスペンスライクな展開で、ハラハラさせられた。 エリザベス・マコンキー《The Departure》から © Mark Senior ブレイ《Making Arrangements》は、ある夫婦の離婚劇を描く。失踪した妻からの手紙を読んで狼狽した夫が、よその男に惹かれる妻の姿を想像して狂気を帯びていくさまを音楽でなぞる。緊張感が張り詰めるなか、ときおり現れる女中のコミカルさに息をつく。ピット内はマコンキー作品よりさらに小編成だが、ドラマティックな音楽に飲み込まれた。 休憩を挟んだ後は、ランゲル《Four Sisters》。ニューヨークを舞台に、亡くなった父の遺産を巡って異母姉妹が攻防を繰り広げる。遺産の内容次第で姉妹の命運は変わる。ロサンゼルスに行きたい、モスクワは嫌、など行き先ごとにいかにも“それっぽい”音楽に立ち替わるのが滑稽だが、嫌いにはなれない。歌手たちもこの日でいちばん思い切りのよい演技で、朗々と声が出ていた。とくにいちばん上の姉オルガを演じたジンウェン・カイ（Ms）とメイド役のハンナ・エドマンズ（S）が魅せた。 ブリテン・シンフォニアがブリテン作品を中心に英国内ツアー ブリテン・シンフォニアはこの翌週にはピットを出て、ブリテンによる歌と弦楽合奏のための《イリュミナシオン》を担いで英国内ツアーを行った。5月16日はロンドンのキングス・クロス駅にほど近い音楽ホール、キングス・プレイスにて、ブリテンがアメリカ滞在中（1939-42）に書いた作品と、影響を与えあった同時代の作曲家作品とを併せたプログラムを実施。 まずはブリテンの弦楽合奏とピアノのための《若きアポロ》で幕開け。ヒュー・ワトキンスのみずみずしいピアノがそのままソロでポール・ボウルズ（1910-99）「6つの前奏曲」をなぞる。そして目玉のブリテン《イリュミナシオン》では、エリザベス・ワッツ（S）のオペラ的規模の歌唱に会場が揺れた。弦楽合奏を背負ってパワフルに物語を動かす歌唱は、歌劇そのものである。 休憩後のコープランド「クラリネット協奏曲」は、2022年ニールセン国際コンクール覇者のオレグ・シェベタ=ドラガンを独奏に迎えた。よく準備された演奏は緻密で正確、さらに柔軟性を得たらより華やかに聞こえるだろう。最後に管楽器を迎えて、同じくコープランドの《アパラチアの春》組曲を九重奏版で。ゾーイ・ベイヤーズ（vn）のリードとワトキンスのピアノに導かれ、楽団はよくドライヴしていた。

items.body: The concept of virtuosity is often misunderstood as an outsized display of technique. In truth though, by definition and in reality, it's about mastery. Such expertise is just as likely to be shown in measured command as it is to appear as fireworks, and this absorbing duo date is a firm reminder of that fact. Legendary bassist Ron Carter and eminent guitarist Yotam Silberstein each possess extraordinary skills and have the wisdom and experience to know when not to flaunt them. That balance between sparkle and spare elegance is what makes Duets such a delight to behold. Crafted in part as a tribute to the late Jim Hall and a nod to the Carter-Hall partnership—and recorded, by divine coincidence, on Hall's birthday—this music, nevertheless, speaks to its own creative duo-logue. Across eight performances, Carter and Silberstein traverse styles, language and states of being. Opening on "Nova Ilusão," this pair demonstrates the draw of a gentle Brazilian sway. Carter's work is supportively buoyant, his note choices providing better direction than any compass could, and Silberstein's melodic suggestions and flourishes mesh beautifully with his low-end companion's perfectly placed lines. "Love Letter" swings and sings brighter than many a take on that Victor Young and Edward Heyman classic. Carter delivers a walk to remember, Silberstein shines with both single note splendors and quality chording, and all is right and tight in the flow. Two Silberstein tunes—the album's only originals—follow that opening diptych and prove complementary. "Blues for Brother Malone," dedicated to noted guitarist Russell Malone, a longtime member of Carter's musical circle who passed away while on tour with the bassist in 2024, lives in the composer's and honoree's shared wheelhouse. Tempo and tone are all about downhome sophistication, a "Sonnymoon for Two" quote serves as the baton handoff between solos, and an earthy grace prevails at every turn. "Rain Again," in a different vein, is purity in precipitation and conversational blend. "The Lamp is Low," born in the '30s and bound to Ravel-ian influence, offers energy without ego. Both musicians find a swinging stride and pace each other throughout. Vernon Duke and Yip Harburg's "What Is There To Say?," another standard drawn from the same era, is firm finesse close to the heart. In both tracks/cases, Carter and Silberstein captivate by finding something new to say in the most well-worn of settings. Irving Berlin's "They Say It's Wonderful," in penultimate placement, unfolds with sprightly significance, reflecting its own aura and optimism through singing strings. Then it's a bop-leaning bon voyage in the form of tenor saxophone slinger Johnny Griffin's "Mil Dew." A lively and interactive exit, this performance affirms what can be heard all across Duets—virtuosity in its truest form.

items.body: Chicago-based trumpeter and composer Rich Willey oversees an impressive eleven-piece ensemble on Best Laid Plans, which embodies seven of his melodically enticing and rhythmically strong compositions, all neatly arranged by Wally Minko. The one clear drawback in this otherwise pleasing session, however, is an incessant rock beat, which lends an aura of sameness to every number that serves to weaken its purpose and impede even the most valiant efforts to separate it from the herd. That is countered to some extent by the inclusion of John Swana's EVI (electric valve instrument), whose unique solo voice adds welcome variety on most tracks. On balance, however, the EVI, even though invigorating, is unable to neutralize the adverse effects of the constant and repetitive drumbeat. Once past that, the music is by and large admirable: engaging melodies, well-drawn charts, forceful blowing by the ensemble, earnest solos by Willey, Swana, pianist (and organist) Paul Mutzabaugh, trombonist Steve Duncan and soprano saxophonist Jim Gailloretto. Willey composed every song including "That's My Little Girl," the lone exception to the funky two-beat format. He and Swana are especially impressive on "Long Lost Brothers," sharing the melodic chores before trading elegant solos. Mutzabaugh solos there too, as he does (on Hammond) on the frisky opener, "Laid Back," and (electric) piano on "My Little Girl." Swana is suitably bracing and ethereal whenever he solos, which is on five of the album's seven numbers; he sits out only on the well-named "Relax & Take It Easy" and similarly even-tenpered "Ladies First." The rhythm section is fine, and one can hardly blame drummer Charles Heath for the annoying drum play; he was only doing what was asked of him. On balance, a well-above-average session whose many charming moments far outweigh the ill-advised choice to set most of them to undue and less-than-engaging rhythms. Earnestly recommended for its many positive aspects.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由芝加哥小号手兼作曲家里奇·威利带领十一人乐团呈现，收录七首原创作品，由沃利·明科负责编曲。音乐整体旋律吸引人，节奏强劲，编曲结构清晰，乐手独奏表现扎实。专辑中引入约翰·斯瓦纳的电声阀门乐器，为多数曲目增添了音色变化。主要问题在于全程贯穿的摇滚节奏型较为单一，削弱了作品之间的区分度。唯一例外是曲目《那是我小女孩》，跳脱了原本的放克两拍框架。节奏组表现稳定，鼓手按照要求完成演奏。整体属于传统爵士大乐队的现代演绎，与实验、前卫或电子音乐路线差距较大。

items.body: Jah Bast wrote “Shadow of the Future” the day his son was born. Geneva’s Bastien Oberhuber, a Rastafarian singer, multi-instrumentalist and producer, records raw roots reggae on analog tape in his own Time & Place studio, playing almost every instrument himself. The double A-side came out on 1 May 2026 on Jah Bast’s own label Time and Place Records, paired with “Daughter’s Ode.” One-drop roots, slow and heavy, the whole thing built around Samuel Ricucci‘s drum foundation and a bass sitting deep in the tape. The title reaches into Rastafari reading of time: “Shadow of the Future” is the long reach of what we do now into the world a child will inherit. “Daughter’s Ode” on the flip features cellist Delphine Goldschmidt-Clermont, the arrangement stripped back around her. items.body: The Spanish group Culture Kultür has been active since the early ’90s and experienced its heyday during the Future-Pop craze. “Atomic” is their first brand-new studio album since “Humanity” in 2019. Last year, however, they released a sort of retrospective record with “Time”. “Atomic” quickly makes it clear that Future-Pop still has a future — or rather, that there are still artists exploring the genre further and achieving high-quality results. The album builds upon the solid foundations these Spaniards laid years ago. The music is highly danceable and features strong choruses that elevate the songs to another level. Elements of Dance, Trance, and dark Electro-Pop occasionally surface, blending seamlessly with the Future-Pop style. While the record does not necessarily sound groundbreaking, Culture Kultür delivers a very polished and refined production. Add to that the excellent vocal production, and you get an album filled with potential hits, some of which were already clearly foreshadowed by the previously released singles. “Atomic” is an album that will get people dancing and put a smile on their faces. As far as I’m concerned, it comes highly recommended for fans of the genre. (Rating:8½). Watch the clip “Atomic Radio”:

items.body:
You'd be forgiven for thinking horsegiirL was some kind of joke. Blame it on mortal prejudice, but it's easy to see an equine humanoid making waves in club culture and write it off as performance art. The evidence certainly skews in that direction: in 2022, first, there was the  breakthrough set  where she wore a tank top emblazoned with the slogan (confession?) "I am a horse, not a DJ," swiftly followed by viral TikTok stormer " My Barn, My Rules. " Since then, countless buzzy  interviews  winking through the screen. For a project so balled up in spectacle, horsegiirL's ascendancy has almost been hijacked by the reams of internet discourse.

Almost.  Nature Is Healing , her debut album, puts to rest any notion that Stella Stallion (AKA horsegiirL) is a clickbaity troll or one-note stunt. This is a full-length of consummate musicianship, interpolating decades' worth of Eurotrash, heavy techno and glossy pop into a rich, oaty feed. For an unstuffy listener with a predilection for something  fun , the album of the summer is here. 

Working with a stable that includes A.G. Cook, Casey MQ, Margo XS, and Nomak—producers whose combined resumes boast the likes of  Charli xcx ,  Oklou , and Kim Petras—means that  Nature Is Healing  sounds expensive. This pedigree might also have you believe that this is going to be a classic hyperpop party, and at first, it seems like that. The queasy, helium-laced, sing-song taunts of album-opener "351%" ("If I was a symphony, it would be a bop") gives way to the controlled-chaos cacophony of "that's my beach!" a paean to tan lines and shaking ass which alternates between music-box keyboard lines and skull-crushing synths with a few dolphin barks thrown in for good measure.

After the hyperpop of its opening one-two punch,  Nature Is Healing  switches up. There's  the breezy Eurodance of "hands hands hands," with an accordion line that immediately transports you to the heyday of late 2000s chart-toppers; the saxophone-heavy "connect the dots," which stays  just  on the right side of cheesy and is easy to imagine blasting out of open windows on long coastal drives for years to come; as well as "only the best," which comes off like Kylie Minogue with a knack for panpipe solos. A few tracks later, she canters to another field entirely, with the '90s-throwback, R&B-esque saxophone over excoriations of a lover stealing her heart. 

This cornucopia of genre references might make for whiplash, but this isn't her first rodeo. But this also gets to the heart of the horsegiirL paradox: she is so defined as being of the moment, that it can be hard to imagine her record having staying power beyond our current zeitgeist. Does the lower energy on "rivers run free" really add that much to the current trip hop revival, for example? Will future generations really chime with the Zoomer overdrive of "AURA?"

But horsegiirL's staying power emerges when she shows off her wide, varied knowledge of dance music. Take "an apple a day," which starts out as an old-school  electroclash  barnburner, campily rapping the varieties of apples before morphing into a frenetic gabber stomper, mixing in the crunch of an apple and a freakishly-paced piano line into its soundboard. In this skull-crushing climax, a vocoded robot voice intones "I'm so angry, I'm the doctor. No one needs me, I'm the doctor." The joke speaks for itself.

Suffice to say,  Nature Is Healing  is a good-times album, a pleasuredome of hedonist joy. Yet expectations that will enrage as much as it delights are wide of the mark. While she might not take herself too seriously–oftentimes the ecstasy of a dance floor is all the message you need—these are still serious works of contemporary, dance floor-angled pop. When the strobes cool down, you might even have the balladry of the title track ringing in your ear. Over a web of downtempo drums and chill out room field recordings, horsegiirL delivers an affecting mission statement: "I just want to dedicate this song to every single creature, every plant, every little bug on this beautiful big planet. You're amazing." Winking, perhaps. Earnest, undeniably.

items.artist: 9128.live still streaming, ambient adjacent music, free, 24
items.body:
Our radio station project, 9128.live is still alive and kicking. Crazy to think it’s been 6 years now since we launched. I recently stumbled into someone at a show who was with us for our all-weekend takeovers during the pandemic era, and he said it helped him get through one of the hardest times of his life. It was very humbling to hear, and despite rarely hearing these comments, it’s one of the reasons I still keep this thing alive. 

 I’m quietly updating music in the background on the station - of course, ASIP music is easy for me to keep updated in rotation, and a few other labels keep on top of things with new releases. without much fanfare. 

 Here are a few key updates that you might have missed: 

 New label partners 

 In the past year or so, we’ve added three amazing catalogs into rotation, including Quiet Details (just this week), Never Late, and Analog Attic. Between these 3 labels alone, we’re hosting some of the most majestic music to hit our ears in recent years. I’m also adding some one-off artist music into rotation, as some listeners get in touch with their own music that fits. 

 Memberships 

 We had a membership that enabled paying users to access unreleased and exclusive sets. I let this dwindle for far too long, so I’m sorry to anyone who kept going with it. But I’ve now canceled it fully as I don’t see the time or space to make this worthwhile right now. Thank you to everyone who helped us keep the station going with their contributions. 

 Listening apps 

 Not new news, but very importantly, we have both iOS and Android apps that enable you to listen to the stream, and they also host the isolatedmix series as a podcast too. A few other bells and whistles to check out too. Links to the apps here. 

 Sonos 

 One of my favorite ways to listen is actually through Sonos (at night) and it’s not too easy to make that happen. But essentially, you need to add the stations custom listen URL into your TuneIn app (once downloaded), then add the TuneIn Service to Sonos, and it should then show in your faves. See here for more ways to listen. 

 The 9128 label 

 When we had regular weekend takeovers, artists were preparing sets for their slots, many of which were original, so we decided to release some of these sets and begin the label. Check out the releases here , by Jo Johnson & Hilary Robinson, Gailes, 36 and Ameeva. With no pipeline for original releases, the label is on a bit of a hiatus, but I hope to spin this up again one day and may open up the catalog to live releases in general. 

 The future 

 Being transparent, the radio costs thousands of dollars to run and host each year. For now, it’s an investment and a bit of a vanity project because I use it so much myself. So a big thank you to everyone who donates to help with this cost. I hope I get to spend more time on the project in the near future, and bring back proper programming and weekend takeovers again. Until then, I’m doing my best to keep the lights on and keeping 24/7 ambient and electronic music flowing. 

 Thanks for tuning in.
